title: Average Australian Salary: How to Convert Your Hourly Rate to Annual Pay
description: Learn how to convert your hourly rate to an annual salary using the 38-hour week, plus tax and super. Understand the average Australian salary from ABS data.
salarySummary: For a full-time worker on 38 hours per week, annual gross pay is hourly rate × 38 × 52, and the ABS average weekly ordinary-time earnings for full-time adults was $2,083.70 per week in May 2026.

faqs.q: How do I convert my hourly rate to an annual salary?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work per week, then by 52 weeks. For a standard full-time week of 38 hours, the formula is: hourly rate × 38 × 52. This gives your gross annual pay before tax and super. Remember that this assumes you work the same hours every week with no unpaid overtime or penalty rates.

faqs.q: What is the average Australian salary according to the ABS?
faqs.a: The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) Average Weekly Earnings for May 2026 show full-time adult ordinary-time earnings of $2,083.70 per week, which equates to about $108,352 per year. However, this is an average across all industries and states, not the median for any specific job. For all employees (including part-time), total average weekly earnings were $1,579.20.

faqs.q: How is superannuation calculated on top of my salary?
faqs.a: Superannuation guarantee is 12% of your ordinary earnings, paid by your employer on top of your salary. For example, if your annual gross salary is $60,000, your employer would contribute an additional $7,200 in super, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. Super is not deducted from your pay; it is an extra benefit.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding Your Annual Pay from an Hourly Rate

If you're paid by the hour or considering a salary offer, converting your hourly rate to an annual figure helps you compare jobs and plan your finances. The standard formula used across Australia is simple: **hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks**. For a full-time employee working 38 hours per week (the ordinary hours under the Fair Work Act), this becomes:

**Annual gross pay = hourly rate × 38 × 52**

For example, if you earn $30 per hour, your annual gross pay would be $30 × 38 × 52 = $59,280. This calculation assumes you work the same number of hours every week, with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. It's a useful starting point, but your actual pay may vary if you work different hours or receive additional loadings.

### The National Minimum Wage and Award Rates

The Fair Work Commission sets the National Minimum Wage each year. From 1 July 2026, the minimum is **$26.44 per hour**, which gives a weekly wage of $1,004.90 for 38 hours and an annual gross of about $52,255. If you are a casual employee, you are entitled to a 25% casual loading on top, making the minimum casual rate **$33.05 per hour**. Many industries have award rates that are higher than the minimum, so always check your specific award or agreement.

When using our [the timesheet](/) to calculate your annual pay, you type your base hourly rate. If you are a casual, tick the box to add 25% casual loading – do not type a rate that already includes the loading.

### The Average Australian Salary: What the ABS Says

The phrase **average australian salary** often refers to the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) Average Weekly Earnings data. For May 2026, the ABS reported:
- **Full-time adult ordinary-time earnings**: $2,083.70 per week (about $108,352 per year)
- **All employees total earnings** (including part-time): $1,579.20 per week (about $82,118 per year)

These are averages across all industries and states, not the median for any particular job. If you are looking for a specific occupation's pay, you should consult industry-specific surveys or award rates. The [reference tables](/data) on this site provide more detailed breakdowns by industry and state.

### Fortnightly and Fortnightly Pay

Many employers pay fortnightly (every two weeks). Your fortnightly gross pay is simply your weekly pay multiplied by 2. For example, if your weekly pay is $1,200, your fortnightly gross is $2,400. This can be helpful when budgeting or comparing with salary offers that are quoted fortnightly.

### Tax and Medicare Levy

Your annual gross pay is not what you take home. The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) applies a progressive tax scale for residents in 2026–27:
- Nil tax on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

In addition, most residents pay a Medicare levy of 2% of taxable income (with reductions for low-income earners). The tax and Medicare are deducted from your pay by your employer through the PAYG system. For an estimate of your take-home pay, see our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) page.

### Superannuation: Paid on Top

Your employer must pay superannuation guarantee contributions of 12% of your ordinary earnings, on top of your salary. This is not deducted from your pay. For example, if your annual gross salary is $80,000, your employer adds $9,600 in super, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. Super is paid into a fund of your choice and is generally not accessible until retirement. Learn more about [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging).

### Important Notes and Limitations

The annual pay shown here is an estimate based on the formula hourly × hours per week × 52. It assumes:
- The same rate every week
- No unpaid overtime
- No penalty rates or allowances
- No salary sacrifice

Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax uses the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. Medicare uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 reduction thresholds were not confirmed here. HELP, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not deducted. This is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax.

For more detailed guidance, refer to the [pay guides](/blog) and [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) pages on this site.
